disclosure.title: Confidentiality and Disclosure Note
disclosure.text: I conducted the following four projects through Duke University collaborations from September 2023 to September 2026. Partner names and proprietary internal system identifiers are withheld under nondisclosure agreements. The collaborators include a leading multimodal foundation model developer, a frontier AI research laboratory, and a leading global alternative asset manager with more than $300 billion in assets under management. The project titles, my role as a researcher, locations, dates, system architectures, mathematical formulations, and reproducible synthetic benchmarks are cleared for public disclosure.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Foundation Model Developer
entries.summary: Sending the riskiest submissions to review concentrates expert attention where errors are most likely, but the uncorrected review results overstate the batch's defect rate. I separated the two things a review buys, information about the whole batch and repair of the data that ships, and derived the allocation each one calls for. The design coordinated more than 300 specialists on weekly batches of over 10,000 tasks and was reused in later post-training programs.
entries.detailTitle: Large-Scale Domain Expert Feedback Governance and Adaptive Review

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **I formulated expert review as a statistical decision problem in which each review has two separate values: what it reveals about the quality of the batch, and what it repairs in the data that ships.** The formulation took shape in late 2023, and I kept refining it as the program grew. For each task I defined an *initial error risk* ($q_i$), the *statistical information value of an independent reference audit* ($m_i / c_i$), and the *expected defect loss removable through additional human handling* ($\Delta_i = r_{i0} - r_{i1}$). A high-risk task can be worth little to audit and little to repair, so the three quantities call for different uses of the same expert capacity.

**I derived the allocation each value calls for and joined them in one batch-level program.** Audit probabilities follow a clipped square-root rule in residual second moment and cost, which gives a design-unbiased quality estimate at minimum variance when the residuals are correctly specified. I optimized remediation assignments against expected defect loss and review cost under specialist-capacity constraints. A batch-level mixed-integer convex program then joins the two, minimizing delivered defect loss subject to a precision ceiling on the quality estimate and a total cost budget.

**The framework supported a program of more than 300 domain experts across several specialties and an external vendor network, and later post-training programs reused its design.** I led its development and defined the mathematical specifications and operating standards for task organization, reliability calibration, acceptance adjudication and review allocation. Those procedures made distributed expert judgments traceable and open to calibration as post-training feedback.

**I designed tiered review rules from Beta-Binomial reliability posteriors, credible intervals, verified sample counts and task-level risk priors.** In one workflow, a flagged submission was dynamically assigned to three additional specialists, and an initially accepted one went to one or two. Expert adjudications fed back into the system, updating contributor reliability posteriors, informing targeted coaching and adjusting review intensity.

**I paired independent random reference audits with escalation of high-risk tasks, so quality could still be measured while review concentrated on the hardest work.** Recurring annotator disagreements became explicit acceptance criteria. I separated missing context from ambiguous instructions and from contributor errors, then revised the task instructions, boundary cases and shared calibration anchors accordingly. Later comparisons against reviewer-error and cost-sensitive deferral models informed the escalation thresholds.

**I built the SQL and Python pipelines behind the allocation solvers.** They brought together task metadata, review histories, acceptance outcomes, turnaround times and behavioral logs, and reconciled platform activity with the team's KPI monitoring system. From these records the solvers took empirical estimates of unit verification costs ($c_i$), task-stratum latencies ($t_{iaj}$) and hard specialist capacity limits ($H_j^{\text{review}}$). I also translated client-reported model defects into reproducible engineering investigations and standard operating procedures.

**I showed in a stratified synthetic experiment with 10,000 submissions that routing audits to the highest predicted risk measures quality worse than sampling at random at the same expected budget.** The uncorrected error rate in the audited queue read **19.60%** where the constructed batch had a defect rate of 7.10%. Inverse-probability correction removed that bias, but the corrected estimate had **33.77%** more variance than under uniform sampling. Allocating by residuals and costs cut the variance by **17.79%** relative to uniform sampling under ideal residual calibration, across 200,000 independent Monte Carlo repetitions. In a separate worked example with 200 tasks, ranking reviews by marginal gain left 41 expected errors where ranking by initial risk left 45.

problemAndApproach.title: Problem and Approach
problemAndApproach.text: In late 2023 I started from a question about expert capacity: how should a post-training program spend a limited pool of reviewers when each review does two jobs at once? A review reveals something about the quality of the whole batch, a correction improves the data that ships, and those two values call for different allocations of the same capacity. High-risk routing shows the tension. When review succeeds in targeting the tasks with higher true error probabilities, the resulting selection bias is positive ($\operatorname{Cov}(\pi(X), q(X)) > 0$), so the raw inspection error rate overstates the defect rate of the batch. The framework I built measures quality through independent audits with design-based correction, optimizes review assignments against expected defect loss and cost under hard capacity limits, and takes its costs and capacities from production records. It coordinated hundreds of distributed specialists and external vendor queues, and I kept refining its specifications as later programs took it up. The seven sections below set out the formal design and its place in the related literature.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Foundation Model Developer
entries.summary: When a synthetic financial case changes one number, its reference answer, the evidence behind that answer and the expert's preference can all go stale together. I built the rules that decide when each has to be recomputed, and the generators that keep accounting identities exact as the data scales. I created Batch Zero to test those rules on domain experts before a task family scaled, and the partner company subsequently adopted the protocol across other post-training programs.
entries.detailTitle: Financial Task Design and Synthetic Data Engineering

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **I framed the scaling of financial training data as a problem of keeping its supervision valid.** When a financial scenario changes, its reference conclusion, supporting evidence and expert preference can all stop being correct together. From late 2023 I treated those four objects and the dependencies among them as a single design problem, and I refined the framework through the programs that followed. For a frontier foundation model program I specified the capability taxonomy, primary evidence standards, input schemas, decisive variables and acceptance criteria. The diagnostic cases targeted high-stakes business decision boundaries where foundation models and practitioners repeatedly make errors, and they translated doctoral or CFA-level domain judgment into testable task requirements.

**I tied reference recomputation to the decision margin of each synthetic variant.** Margin conditions certify when the decision label remains unchanged; reference calculations, supporting evidence and pairwise preferences are checked separately. Gaussian margin-to-noise analysis ($\gamma/s$) measures the label-flip risk. When a perturbation approaches or crosses a decision boundary, the workflow recomputes the reference solution and collects new five-level preference judgments on fresh model reasoning.

**I designed a five-level pairwise preference protocol for RLHF and DPO supervision.** It records why an expert prefers one response to another. Each judgment has to cite verifiable evidence, the relevant accounting rules and the decisive variables, so the preference reaches post-training with its reasons attached and helps train models to assess whether a financial judgment has sufficient support.

**I created Batch Zero to establish and refine these standards, and the partner company subsequently adopted the protocol across other post-training programs.** Starting from the capability objectives and data requirements of post-training research teams, I established a protocol for independent execution and expert calibration that a task family goes through before it enters large-scale data construction. Doctoral-level domain experts independently construct tasks, generate synthetic variants, solve reference cases and assign five-level pairwise preference scores. The disagreements and failure modes that appear in execution inform revisions to task specifications, boundary cases and **Batch One** data acceptance criteria.

**I developed financial synthetic data methods for four settings.** For each task I selected a mathematical generator and adapted it to the task's structural invariants, data types and permitted information:

**I quantified stale-label errors, temporal leakage and task-family clustering.** Analytical derivations and simulations show that when labels are not recomputed, synthetic perturbations near a decision boundary produce **40.13%** inherited-label error at $\gamma/s = 0.25$. Undisclosed Brownian bridge endpoint conditioning creates an apparent **29.29% reduction in RMSE** at the interval midpoint through future-information leakage. With within-family correlation $\rho = 0.5$, 2,000 nominal synthetic variants from 100 task families amount to about **190** effective independent observations.

items: *Cross-sectional corporate fundamentals.* I used Gaussian and vine copulas with conditional sampling for company size, operating history and financial ratios. These methods preserve joint dependencies across columns and avoid the unrealistic combinations that sampling each column independently produces.

*Accounting identities, ratio bounds and chronological order.* Constrained sampling, variable transformations and covariance-weighted affine projections enforce balance-sheet and cash-flow identities, ratio ranges and date ordering. Across 200,000 12-dimensional synthetic draws, the maximum constraint residual was **$1.21 \times 10^{-14}$**. A separate standardized-residual rejection model had an acceptance rate of $0.0002529\%$.
*Multimodal records with numerical and categorical fields.* Deep tabular generators model the multimodal empirical distributions, and business-rule checks are mandatory after generation.

*Continuous-time price and interest-rate paths.* SDEs, neural SDEs, Brownian bridges and stochastic interpolation generate paths for temporal financial tasks, and each method is matched to the task's permitted filtration ($\mathcal{F}_s$) to keep future information out of evaluation.

problemAndApproach.title: Problem and Approach
problemAndApproach.text:
In late 2023, frontier foundation models could reproduce corporate finance definitions and still made unpredictable errors in financial workflows, where a small numerical change or an accounting footnote could reverse an investment recommendation. Adding synthetic data helps only if the supervision moves with the scenario. I built the data strategy around that requirement, connecting task specifications, synthesis methods and expert calibration to the capability objectives of post-training research teams and to two problems:
1. **Diagnosing reasoning limits through task design.** I designed prompts around subtle business failure modes, including covenant breaches, off-balance-sheet adjustments and valuation differences close to a decision boundary, because simple prompts may give little basis for telling candidate responses apart. Paired with the five-level preference protocol, these prompts carry a domain judgment such as *"Response A is better because it isolates the working-capital constraint and cites Footnote 4"* into structured preference supervision for post-training.
2. **Matching the generator to the financial structure.** Synthetic financial data has to satisfy structural constraints, stay consistent with reference judgments and respect the task's information boundaries. A corporate table that violates Total Assets $=$ Total Liabilities $+$ Equity, even by a fraction of a percentage point, introduces a structural error. An interest-rate path that exposes a future terminal rate to a historical forecasting task introduces temporal leakage. Sections 1 through 6 give the conditions, analytical results and validation designs for each method. Batch Zero makes these requirements its acceptance criteria: experts have to be able to execute the task specification independently, reproduce reference solutions and calibrate their judgments.

The team averaged roughly 500 completed financial tasks a week, or about 2,000 over a four-week cycle. Each task combined synthetic financial data with a reference solution and expert review. A typical financial task took about three specialist-hours across drafting, three reviews and revision.

entries.organization: Duke University × Frontier AI Research Laboratory
entries.summary: A model can reach the right answer through an unsupported step, and a grader that matches a reference solution will reject a correct proof that takes another route. I wrote an acceptance rule that handles both: a conclusion stands when its assumptions, derivations and execution evidence support it, whichever valid route was taken, and a failed step removes support from everything downstream. Mathematical certificates, LLM-assisted screening and specialist adjudication each check what they are suited to check. On constructed submissions where final-answer matching accepted 75% of the invalid work, the certificate verifier accepted none.
entries.detailTitle: General Reasoning Evaluation and Layered Verification

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **I developed a proof-obligation framework that defines when a model's reasoning should be accepted.** Starting in late 2023, I organized deliverables into dependency graphs ($\Gamma_q \vdash C_q$) that link each conclusion to its domain assumptions, method applicability, evidentiary support, compliant execution, uniform approximation bounds and claimed strength. Valid alternative derivations pass on the same terms as the reference route. When a step fails, the graph locates the first unsupported step and what it affects downstream. For tasks that admit formalization, checking local nodes and their dependencies within a sound inference system establishes the full conclusion.

**I developed checkable error certificates and bounds on solution quality for programmatically verifiable task families.** The projected-residual optimality bound ($0 \le f(x) - v^* \le \|P_{\ker A} r\|_2^2 / (2\mu)$) splits feasibility, stationarity and the accuracy of a conclusion into separate verification obligations, and different proofs can pass by satisfying the same ones. Section 3 gives the assumptions, certificate construction and problem class.

**I established complementary forms of verification across mathematical certificates, code and rule checks, LLM-assisted screening and specialist adjudication, and later programs reused the layered design.** Code checks directly verifiable answers, required deliverables, tool permissions and other requirements specified in advance. LLM-as-a-Judge helps flag missing evidence, misapplied rules and gaps in reasoning, and disputed domain judgments go to scholars with relevant expertise.

**I evaluated answers, visible reasoning and execution evidence together.** I cross-checked the model's displayed CoT against its actual tool calls, return values and intermediate outputs to see whether what it claimed had observable support. From elapsed time, attempt counts and changes in intermediate results I identified repeated operations, continued use of failed assumptions and attempts that added no evidence. Correctness, compliance and efficiency were recorded as separate results, and a resource limit counted toward acceptance only when the task specification set it beforehand.

**I derived how false acceptance ($\alpha$) and false rejection ($\beta$) can reverse model rankings and bias the binary cross-entropy gradient used to train process reward models ($E[\nabla_s \ell(s,V) - \nabla_s \ell(s,Z) \mid h] = p(h) - \tilde{p}(h)$).** In the worked example, models with true validity rates of 72% and 64% score 73.12% and 76.96%, so the weaker one ranks first. I also gave the tolerance-propagation rule ($a\delta + 2\varepsilon$) for bijective task transformations, which says when a transformed task still supports a valid comparison.

**On 3,600 exact-arithmetic submissions from 600 constructed strongly convex quadratic task families, final-answer matching accepted 75.0% of the invalid submissions and strict reference-path matching rejected 50.0% of the valid proofs.** Certificate checking accepted all 1,200 valid proofs and rejected all 2,400 invalid submissions, so strict error detection and acceptance of valid alternative routes held together on the same set.

problemAndApproach.title: Problem and Approach
problemAndApproach.text:
The question I took up in late 2023 was what should entitle a model's reasoning to be accepted. A correct answer can coexist with unsupported assumptions, misapplied rules or tool use that violates the task specification, and a fixed reference path will reject sound work that takes another route. I designed an acceptance rule around proof obligations: a conclusion stands when its assumptions, derivations and execution evidence support it, whichever valid route the model took, and a failed obligation removes support from everything that depends on it. Programmatic certificates discharge checkable obligations, LLM-assisted screening identifies possible gaps, and specialist scholars adjudicate disputed semantic questions. I kept refining the framework through September 2026. Sections 1 through 7 set out the acceptance criteria, the certificates for a programmatically verifiable subfamily, the experiments and the related literature.

The team produced roughly 500 scientific reasoning tasks a week, or about 2,000 over a four-week cycle. Each task included a detailed, step-by-step reference solution and repeated verification of the argument.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Global Alternative Asset Manager
entries.summary: Due diligence has more facts to check than analyst time to check them. I built a method that determines which investment conclusions the evidence in hand already supports and which single fact is most valuable to verify next, with ranking guarantees that hold across every near-optimal scoring model and every admissible resolution of the unverified evidence. It was implemented with a leading global alternative asset manager and reused in subsequent research.
entries.detailTitle: Evidence Verification and Robust Comparison in Investment Research
keyContributions: **I framed investment due diligence as a decision problem: which conclusions does the current evidence support, and which fact is most valuable to verify next?** The framework took shape in late 2023, and I refined it through the work that followed. I represented unresolved evidence $\mathcal{X}(E)$ jointly with a near-optimal model set $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ through $\Omega(E) = \mathcal{F}_\alpha \times \mathcal{X}(E)$ and derived convex support-function bounds ($h_U(a_f)$) that give ranking guarantees across every retained model and admissible resolution of the evidence. Under the same affine scoring model, common measurement errors cancel when the two companies have identical exposures. In a synthetic comparison, the joint model certified a 0.6-point advantage that the difference bound from separate company intervals ($[-1.4, 2.6]$) could not show.

**I derived a query criterion that ranks verification by its effect on the decision.** It prioritizes the reduction in worst-case decision regret that a query can guarantee and needs no probability distribution over the scenarios inside the specified joint uncertainty set. For unequal query costs, $V(q)/c_q$ gives a one-step efficiency measure. In a worked example with eight scenarios and one equal-cost query, targeted verification cut worst-case regret from 0.61 score units to zero, whereas rechecking an already verified feature with a large SHAP attribution reduced regret by zero.

**I implemented the framework with a leading global alternative asset manager, and subsequent research reused it.** Institutional diligence requirements became measures of score reliability, pairwise ranking stability and verification priority. The workflow ingests evidence, scores companies across a set of near-optimal models, computes ranking bounds and allocates verification effort by minimax regret. Each correction triggers rescoring and attribution updates, so the investment committee has a traceable basis for its analysis.

**I showed where conventional bootstrap resampling, and verification priorities based on raw SHAP magnitudes, fail when inputs contain shared reporting bias or unverified claims.** Under a fixed common bias, a nominal 95% interval loses coverage as the sample grows, and resampling the same records cannot identify the bias. A self-reported metric near the sector mean can carry a near-zero attribution and still hold enough unresolved error to reverse a ranking. Verification value needs its own calculation.

**I studied what AI-polished corporate narratives do to LLM-assisted scoring, ESG ratings and investment analysis when the claims underneath them lack factual support.** I converted operating reports, audited financial statements, sustainability disclosures, management questionnaires and third-party datasets into structured scoring rules that carry source and version records. AI-assisted checks then pick out unsupported claims and contradictions across documents, and shared reporting errors enter the same review, so that verification in private-market and ESG research can be targeted.

**I deployed gradient-boosted trees and deep tabular models to capture nonlinear thresholds and interactions, and measured how far their explanations depend on model choice.** Attributions computed across the near-optimal set $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$, read together with conditional analysis of correlated features, identify the scoring factors whose contributions stay stable across models.

problemAndApproach.title: Problem and Approach
problemAndApproach.text: Due diligence has a limited budget of analyst time and a long list of facts that could be checked. In late 2023 I began treating that as a decision problem: given the evidence in hand, which conclusions does it support, and which single fact would most improve the decision if it were verified? AI-polished narratives, unverified sustainability claims and common reporting errors can all move ESG and investment scores, so the answer has to account for uncertainty in the corporate evidence as well as in the scoring models. The architecture I developed takes a traceable evidence state as its input and builds in model multiplicity, joint measurement error and the costs of verification, and I kept refining it through 2026. Sections 1 through 6 develop the limits of attribution methods, the joint uncertainty model, ranking bounds, the query criterion, versioned updates and analytical benchmarks.

entries.summary: I built the data and ranking system behind Jiritsu's partnerships for its asset-verification and privacy-preserving computation services, as the sole dedicated contributor for new issuers. I reported to co-founder Asher Gottesman and ran core-team reviews with technical and financial guidance from Gene Itkis of MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Michael Lustig, former Senior Managing Director at BlackRock. The work combined data engineering, preference ranking, and counterparty discussions, and it ended in partnership recommendations to the board.
keyContributions: I was the sole dedicated contributor to business development for new issuers, reporting to co-founder Asher Gottesman. I turned commercialization priorities into screening criteria, experiments, data requirements, and outreach plans, and independently managed analysis, counterparty discussions, and recommendations.

I organized core-team reviews with commercial input from Asher Gottesman and technical and financial guidance from Gene Itkis of MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Michael Lustig, former Senior Managing Director at BlackRock and Adjunct Professor of Finance at NYU Stern. In these reviews, I assessed applied cryptography, zero-knowledge applications, technical fit, liquidity, and risk.

I designed a two-stage framework for real-world assets, stablecoins, DeFi, and infrastructure: it tests identity, liquidity, pricing validity, data completeness, and risk, then ranks commercial fit and accessibility. I used issuer-level error analysis to refine qualification rules, exclude out-of-scope projects, and record evidence-backed reasons for each decision.

I resolved issuer identities across CoinGecko, chain records, websites, white papers, and disclosures, and reconciled multichain listings and wrapped or bridged assets to remove duplicate opportunities. I then built market and text features spanning liquidity, capitalization, activity, project age, chain affiliation, business models, and technical needs.

I built a Python, Prefect, DuckDB, and Parquet pipeline for ingestion, standardization, entity mapping, feature preparation, and querying, with scheduled refreshes, retries, persisted outputs, reruns, and historical backfills to support model training and repeatable shortlist updates.

I trained a LightGBM pairwise ranking model on the core team's comparisons of eligible counterparties, combining commercial, disclosure, and market features to prioritize approximately 800 potential partners. I repeated comparison, retraining, and ranking over two to four weeks, using uncertainty sampling to focus expert review on borderline candidates, near ties, and conflicting evidence.

I applied issuer similarity analysis and Leiden community detection to discover overlooked projects with related business or technical characteristics, then brought qualified candidates into commercial review and ranking.

I screened 18,000+ token records into approximately 800 potential counterparties, 30 outreach priorities, and six proposed pilot counterparties. I discussed asset-verification needs, service arrangements, and technology licensing with prospects, and delivered the candidate list and commercial assessments to the board for technical and business evaluation.

entries.summary: I led the China workstream of a global market-entry engagement covering China, Japan, and the Middle East for a premium European appliance brand. I analyzed approximately 50,000 e-commerce listings alongside consumer evidence and policy research to recommend local products, pricing, channels, and marketing while maintaining the client's global positioning.
entries.detailTitle: China Market Entry for a Premium European Appliance Brand
keyContributions: I built a MECE analytical framework spanning product fit, pricing, channels, marketing, and policy, defining which elements of the client's premium positioning should remain consistent globally and where the China strategy required local adaptation.

I specified data requirements across five e-commerce platforms and seven appliance categories, coordinating with data scientists on collection and local analysts on validation. I owned downstream processing and interpretation of approximately 50,000 listings in Python, standardizing attributes, efficiency labels, prices, promotions, and reviews while preserving channel-specific observations.

I mapped competitors in Tableau by category, price band, efficiency, and features. Combining product comparisons with consumer reviews, I identified relatively underserved segments, including high-efficiency products at mid- to high-price points, and assessed opportunities in tier-1 and tier-2 cities.

I evaluated the European portfolio against Chinese usage needs, product dimensions, and efficiency requirements. I recommended local assortments and compared the brand's website, e-commerce, physical retail, and channel partnerships, incorporating Xiaohongshu and Douyin into marketing analysis.

I researched efficiency standards, subsidies, certification, and market access through published sources and expert interviews, including think-tank discussions. I built entry scenarios by category and city tier, translating current requirements and expected policy changes into product-introduction and timing recommendations.

I delivered the China market report and represented the workstream in global project meetings, presenting the evidence behind product, pricing, channel, and marketing recommendations and coordinating green-product definitions and policy assumptions. I documented field mappings and processing rules in a reusable template for subsequent regional analysis.
I received a full-time offer from Euromonitor's consulting team during the internship.

entries.summary: I applied statistical methods to sustainability assessment and green-credit screening within China Construction Bank's internal framework. I combined company data, historical assessments, and explicit eligibility rules to support candidate review, then documented the method for product managers and risk officers evaluating its use on a platform.
entries.detailTitle: PCA-Based Sustainability Analysis and Green-Credit Screening
keyContributions: I analyzed financial, operational, and environmental data for approximately 2,000 entities within CCB's framework of more than 30 indicators, assessing overall scores alongside minimum requirements for individual metrics.

I used PCA to identify overlapping indicator information and construct compact representations for candidate comparison. I applied supervised learning to historically labeled cases, examining feature patterns associated with positive and negative assessments and adding empirical evidence to candidate assessment.
I incorporated life cycle assessment principles into sustainability analysis, examining operating and environmental factors alongside financial performance.
I tested the initial top 30% of ranked candidates against individual-metric and overall-score minimums, retaining approximately 28% of the full pool for further research and review.

I reviewed selection and exclusion patterns across the pool, separating ranking cutoffs from threshold failures, and converted borderline cases, unmet requirements, and follow-up questions into a reusable checklist linked to the applicable screening rules.
I delivered a methodology note explaining scoring logic, data sources, model behavior, and edge cases to product managers and risk officers assessing the method for platform use.

entries.organization: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
entries.summary: A spacecraft sometimes has to act before anyone on the ground can approve the command, and waiting carries risks of its own. I formulated a two-threshold test that separates the authority to act from the evidence needed to delegate execution, and applied it to delayed spacecraft operations, orbital avoidance, debris capture, and SETI. I also proposed task-specific authorization records, so that a delegated decision can be examined in advance, revised when its assumptions change, and reconstructed after the event.
entries.detailTitle: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
keyContributions: I specified a two-threshold decision procedure linking legal authority, evidence for delegation, and the time at which human review can still change the outcome, distinguishing individual approval, advance-constrained action, and fallback behavior as separate supervisory choices.

I designed a task-specific authorization record specifying responsible actors, permitted actions, operating conditions, exposed interests, and reassessment triggers, and connected these terms to independent scrutiny and event records that allow consequential decisions to be reconstructed.

I compared delayed spacecraft operations and orbital avoidance against existing automation and ground review, analyzing how latency, uncertain trajectories, simultaneous maneuvers, and failed coordination affect delegation and redistribute risk among operators.

I used debris capture and SETI to distinguish technical capability from permission to affect another party's interests or confirm a scientific interpretation, and proposed scientific verification through alternative explanations, independent observations, and documented evidence.

I integrated review delays, compliance costs, disclosure risks, and correlated failures into the proposed controls. I developed proportionate reassessment around material changes, reusable evidence, and legally competent institutions, making the burdens of supervision part of the authorization decision.

entries.organization: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
entries.summary: A small state can license a launch, own a satellite, or buy a service and still lack the decision it meant to keep. I compared New Zealand's launch regulation, Norway's Arctic satellite partnership, and Luxembourg's LUXEOSys procurement to separate permission, ownership, operational rights, and implementation capacity. I proposed an accountable-acceptance standard for strategic dependencies, which ties interruption powers and response rights to funded capability, and translated it into licensing and procurement terms.
entries.detailTitle: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
keyContributions: I built a structured comparison around specific public functions and the decisions needed to perform them, defining practical autonomy as the capacity to make and implement a specified lawful public decision. I examined external dependencies, legal and operational rights, domestic capability, and documented outcomes to assess whether retained authority could support an actual public decision.

I identified distinct mechanisms in the three cases: retained launch-permission authority in New Zealand, operational capability through divided responsibilities in Norway, and the planning and legislative information required alongside asset ownership in Luxembourg.

I proposed an accountable-acceptance standard requiring decision makers to identify who can interrupt essential services, which information and rights permit a response, and what funded capacity enables action. Material gaps would require reasoned acceptance or revision before commitment.

I translated the standard into proposed licensing and procurement terms covering operator information, significant changes, suspension, recovery, and service transition, and connected these terms to lifetime costs, technical staffing, and timely legislative scrutiny of financial commitments.

I analyzed collective agency through anti-satellite-testing commitments, UN consensus procedures, and ESA programme and voting rules. I distinguished participation rights, influence, and implementation capacity, connecting national safeguards to collective restraint on debris and cross-border service disruption.

entries.organization: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
entries.summary: Who may choose among climate risks for people who cannot leave the resulting climate? I proposed two legal duties for solar geoengineering. Comparative justification connects risk-risk analysis to authorization by requiring proponents to defend their policy alternatives and answer challenges from affected constituencies. Continuity addresses termination risk, which I traced to a separation between political control, operator succession, and the physical cooling trajectory, so that authority can change hands without an abrupt physical stop.
entries.detailTitle: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
keyContributions: I separated historical climate conditions, a future without stratospheric aerosol injection, and feasible policy portfolios as distinct comparators, and analyzed how baseline selection, welfare measures, and distributional assumptions shape the case for intervention and the burdens assigned to exposed populations.

I proposed a comparative justification duty requiring proponents to defend alternatives, disclose distributional choices, and answer substantiated objections, and designed powers for independently selected representatives of exposed constituencies to demand redesign or withhold collective approval.

I developed a continuity duty separating program control, operator choice, and the cooling trajectory. It specifies bounded interim succession, independent monitoring, transition finance, and gradual withdrawal so that political authority can change without automatically triggering abrupt physical cessation.

I mapped environmental assessment, notification, and consultation requirements onto the authorization problem. I distinguished limited research from climate-affecting deployment and proposed scrutiny based on expected effects and cumulative scale, including review of related projects together.

I formulated a priority rule for serious threats to subsistence and survival, requiring comparison of feasible alternatives, shared authorization, and credible relief, and built periodic reassessment of forgone benefits and harms of nondeployment into the same decision process.

entries.organization: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
entries.summary: Restoring a wetland is one decision, and relying on that restoration to permit the loss of another is a second. I compared Florida with the Greater Bay Area on protection, repair, and compensatory mitigation, and used West Lake, Deep Bay, and Hong Kong's 2024 San Tin approval to test what counts as evidence of functional replacement. I proposed site-specific baselines, staged authorization and ecological acceptance, funded correction, and continuing responsibility until the obligation is discharged.
entries.detailTitle: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
keyContributions: I organized the legal comparison around habitat protection, repair, and compensation for new loss, tracing duties, approval instruments, and administrative powers across Florida, mainland China, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, and Macao to identify how restoration conditions can take legal effect.

I used West Lake to examine hydrological rehabilitation and Deep Bay and San Tin to assess functional replacement, distinguishing canopy growth, construction, and predicted enhancement from evidence supporting compensation, including additionality and the timing of replacement functions.

I proposed staged approval and acceptance separating engineering completion from ecological performance. I specified site baselines, functional objectives, monitoring periods, seasonal coverage, and review authority, linking damaging development phases to the availability of the functions used to justify them.

I designed arrangements for delayed or failed recovery through funded monitoring, correction, and continuing management. I distinguished contractor performance from ecological uncertainty and examined retention, financial security, and public budget commitments as instruments for sustaining corrective work.

I linked ecological evidence to fund release, discharge of responsibility, and development permission, proposing smaller footprints, revised sequencing, alternative sites, or refusal to credit compensation where promised functions lack credible replacement, while allowing proportionate trials in degraded habitats.

entries.organization: Jones Lang LaSalle Capital Markets Team
entries.summary: I served as the project team's ESG lead on acquisition advisory for a Southeast Asian conglomerate seeking Chinese office properties. Working with JLL's internal ESG team, I connected asset screening, property valuation, and site-level diligence with the client's investment requirements and potential refurbishment or repositioning plans.
entries.detailTitle: Office Investment Underwriting and ESG Due Diligence
keyContributions: I screened 22 cities across four investable regions against client preferences, preliminary budgets, market liquidity, and institutional-grade office stock, narrowing the search to 20 assets in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, and Chengdu.

I developed a GRESB-informed desktop screen with approximately 40 ESG and operating indicators, coordinating with JLL's internal ESG team. It flagged environmental, operating, and capital-expenditure concerns that excluded approximately 40% of candidates before full valuation and due diligence.

I structured diligence across management, performance, and development: ownership and SPV transparency, policy coverage, compliance, safety, and 12 months of continuous operating records. I benchmarked energy, carbon, water, waste, certifications, and upgrades against comparable properties matched by city, submarket, vintage, and building systems.

I assessed upgrade, refurbishment, and extension risks through capital-expenditure and cash-flow analysis, using equipment age, chiller efficiency, building-management systems, sub-metering, air monitoring, and maintenance records as proxies where utility data were unavailable. I converted findings into red, amber, and green signals and asset-specific diligence priorities.

I underwrote shortlisted properties using discounted cash flow, replacement cost, and comparable transactions, incorporating operating conditions and upgrade requirements into valuation assumptions, cash-flow scenarios, and exit-risk assessments.
I built ten dashboards in Excel, Python, and Tableau to compare market fundamentals, valuations, ESG indicators, and scenario exposures across cities, assets, and the investment pipeline.

I led bilingual briefings for capital-markets leadership and client managers, shaped site-visit sequencing and ESG questions, and delivered standardized asset books covering tenant concentration, weighted average lease expiry, vacancy, rents, operating costs, valuation models, and diligence findings.

entries.summary: Through a Duke Practicum, I led shipping, logistics, and industrial asset-tracking research for Hubble's Bluetooth satellite commercialization. I assessed where the technology's cost, accuracy, power consumption, and periodic reporting capabilities matched customer needs, translating technical and market evidence into recommendations for early applications.
entries.detailTitle: Bluetooth Satellite Commercialization and Market Selection

metadata.position: Student Consultant and Business Analytics Analyst, Duke Practicum

keyContributions: I led the shipping, logistics, and industrial tracking workstreams after Hubble's $20 million Series A and before its first satellite launches, and helped refocus the go-to-market brief on vertical-market selection by organizing opportunity scans, elimination criteria, detailed assessment, market sizing, and prioritization.

I translated stakeholder objectives, company cost data, and technical parameters into application assessments, comparing customer needs, incumbent solutions, accuracy, power consumption, and reporting frequency to identify promising uses for periodic location tracking.

I prepared and conducted workstream interviews through Duke Pratt's alumni network, including sales professionals, contributing to a team research program covering approximately 20 fields, typically two or three alumni per field, and more than 100 hours of expert interviews.

I triangulated Fuqua business databases, official statistics, industry reports, competitor research, and interviews, applying SWOT and PESTLE and contributing market-sizing models, scenario forecasts, and sensitivity analyses to compare priority applications.

I integrated workstream findings into the team's evaluation of approximately 20 use cases, five recommended market directions, and 100-page strategy report, and presented conclusions to management and the board, explaining market attractiveness, competition, and the requirements for commercialization.

entries.summary: I owned public-data research and governance screening for a Greater China dental-investment theme. Working with the VP and investment team, I prioritized subsectors and candidates, then translated governance concerns into investment recommendations, management questions, and on-site diligence priorities.
entries.detailTitle: Dental Investment Research and Governance Due Diligence
keyContributions: I reconciled approximately 2,000 funding cases and 200 regulatory items from about 20 sources, including CVSource, industry reporting, and corporate registries. I deduplicated rounds and standardized entities, subsectors, dates, financing classifications, and currencies, producing 600+ deals and 120–150 actionable regulatory events.

I owned funding-flow, regulatory, industry-structure, and competitive research, comparing orthodontic aligner brands, private dental chains, equipment suppliers, and digital and SaaS providers to inform subsector prioritization.

I worked with the VP and investment team to narrow a longlist of 100+ targets to more than ten candidates. I profiled financing histories, valuation ranges, and investor bases, and assigned pass, watch, or exclude recommendations with regulatory, reputational, shareholder, and supplier-risk flags.

I converted MSCI Corporate Governance and Corporate Behavior topics into ten subcategories and 33 diligence checks covering control complexity, related-party exposure, disclosure, audit quality, and business ethics.

I authored pass, conditional, and deny memoranda to guide diligence depth and valuation discussions, specifying evidence requirements and management questions for governance issues requiring further investigation.

I presented governance and risk findings to partners, prompting two management meetings and additional auditor-tenure checks. I identified accounting and related-party concerns in two finalists and translated them into management questions and on-site diligence priorities.
